newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian government tries to avoid mid-term poll.
newsitem.headline: Indian government tries to avoid mid-term poll.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda began discussions with coalition partners on Monday in a bid to stave off mid-term elections after a key ally withdrew its support for the government.

Sources in the ruling centre-left United Front alliance told Reuters Deve Gowda held talks with senior leaders of the 15-party coalition ahead of a meeting of its decision-making Steering Committee later on Monday.

"The prime minister was assured, and he agreed, that the United Front will continue to be in charge (of the government)," a source close to Deve Gowda said. "There is a crisis which we will overcome, without the need for mid-term elections."
Indian shares plunged more than eight percent in panicky trade on Monday, as investors sold after the Congress Party on Sunday withdrew its 10-month old support for Deve Gowda.
"People are having a big panic," said a chief dealer at a foreign institutional investor.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index dived 313.50 points, or 8.56 percent, to 3,350.03 at the open.

"I met the President (Shankar Dayal Sharma) today and told him that we are withdrawing support to the United Front government and I also staked our claim to form a (new) government," Congress president Sitaram Kesri said on Sunday.
Stockbrokers in Bombay, India's financial centre, said it was unclear how Congress, which has only 140 deputies in the 545-seat Lok Sabha, or lower house, could form a government.
Deve Gowda's alliance, which groups free-traders, communists and centrists and controls some 178 deputies in the lower house, was formed in June 1996 after inconclusive national elections.
An opinion poll last month predicted major gains for the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) against both the United Front and the Congress if mid-term polls were held soon.
Congress politicians said Kesri was expected on Monday to ask President Sharma, the constitutional head of state, for a chance to form a new government.
But officials at the Presidential Palace said Sharma was seeking the advice of legal experts to decide if Kesri had a legitimate claim.
Ram Jethmalani, a lawyer and former minister in a shortlived BJP government, was quoted by state television as saying Sharma should let Deve Gowda seek a vote of confidence in parliament.

Sharma allowed the BJP, with support from 194 deputies, to form a government following inconclusive elections in May, but the party resigned after 12 days when it was unable to muster a majority in parliament.
Parliament is due to decide the fate of the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) when it reconvenes on April 21.

Former Congress finance minister Manmohan Singh said on Sunday that the government would not face a crisis over the budget for four months after parliament passed a vote on account to meet temporary expenses.
Congress leaders said the party could consider amending Deve Gowda's budget if it gets to form a government.
The political crisis has also raised questions about who will be the country's next president.
Sharma's five-year term ends in July when parliament and state legislatures must elect a successor or vote him into a second term.
"For the sake of the budget and the president's election any mid-term poll, if at all necessary, must be held in four months," an official at the Presidential Palace said.
